49502: How the Old and New Testaments fit together, how Jesus and Paul read the Scriptures, and what it means that Jesus is the Word who interprets the words. This unit gives full voice to the “Jesus is perfect theology” reading (Christ as the full revelation of the Father) and sets it beside other Christ-centred readings — Reformed, evangelical, Catholic and Orthodox — with Jewish perspectives and the fair critiques of each.
49503: Old and New: Progressive Revelation (and Progressive Christianity)
49504: How do the Old and New Testaments fit together? Is “progressive revelation” the same thing as liberal or “progressive” Christianity?
49505: The two Testaments tell one story: God spoke truly “in many portions and in many ways”, and then finally and fully in his Son. Progressive revelation means God’s self-disclosure unfolds and reaches its peak in Jesus; progressive Christianity usually means the church’s moral knowledge moves on beyond the text. They are different claims, and most views sit somewhere on a spectrum between them.
49507:
Christians call the two halves of the Bible the Old Testament and the New Testament. “Testament” translates a Latin word for “covenant”. The names come from the Bible itself: Jeremiah promised a “new covenant” written on the heart, and Jesus spoke of the cup at the Last Supper as “the new covenant in my blood”.

The New Testament never treats the Old as a separate religion. It opens with a genealogy that runs from Abraham to Jesus, and it quotes or echoes the Hebrew Scriptures hundreds of times. When Paul says “all Scripture is God-breathed” and “able to make you wise unto salvation”, the Scriptures he means are what we call the Old Testament. Jewish readers rightly point out that “Old” can sound like “out of date”; some Christians therefore say “Hebrew Bible” or “First Testament”. The word “old” here means “first” and “earlier”, not “worthless”.

So the first thing to hold is continuity: one God, one people-story, one promise to bless all nations through Abraham’s family, carried forward to its fulfilment.
49509:
The second thing to hold is newness. Something happens in Jesus that the earlier Scriptures did not contain on their own. John puts it simply: “the law was given by Moses, but grace and truth came by Jesus Christ.” Hebrews says the first covenant is “becoming obsolete” and that the law had “a shadow of good things to come, and not the very image of the things”.

In practice the New Testament reports real changes: animal sacrifice ends because of Christ’s once-for-all offering; food laws no longer divide Jew and Gentile; circumcision is not required of Gentile believers; the people of God is now defined by trust in the Messiah and the gift of the Spirit rather than by ethnic descent. Even Jesus’ first followers found these changes hard (see Peter’s vision in Acts 10 and the Jerusalem council in Acts 15).

The question every Christian tradition has to answer is how continuity and newness fit together. Too much continuity and Christ becomes a footnote to Moses. Too much newness and the Old Testament becomes a different religion with a different God — the error the early church called Marcionism.
49510: “In many portions and in many ways”: progressive revelation
49511:
Hebrews opens with a sentence that frames this whole unit: “God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets, hath in these last days spoken unto us by his Son.” The two Greek words behind “sundry times and divers manners” (*polymerōs* and *polytropōs*) mean “in many parts” and “in many ways”. The earlier word was real, inspired speech from God, but it came in pieces, through many people, in many forms — law, story, poem, vision.

“Progressive revelation” is the theological name for this pattern. It means God made himself known step by step across history, and that later stages clarify and complete earlier ones. Peter says the prophets “searched diligently” about a salvation they did not fully see. Paul speaks of a “mystery” hidden for ages and now revealed. Jesus is the last and fullest word: not one more prophet, but the Son through whom God speaks.

This idea is not new or liberal. Irenaeus in the second century spoke of God training humanity gradually, like a teacher with children. Reformed theologians such as Geerhardus Vos made “progressive revelation” a key idea of biblical theology, and Catholic teaching (*Dei Verbum* 15) speaks of the Old Testament as showing a “divine pedagogy” — God teaching step by step.
49512: Progressive revelation is not the same as progressive Christianity
49513:
The learner’s notes rightly separate two things that are often confused because they share a word.

Progressive revelation says: God’s self-revelation unfolds within Scripture and culminates in Christ. The measure is inside the story — Jesus himself, as the apostles witness to him.

Progressive (or liberal) Christianity is a broad modern movement. Many in it say that the church’s moral and spiritual understanding keeps growing beyond the biblical text, so that some biblical teachings can be set aside in the light of modern knowledge, experience and reason. Thinkers such as Marcus Borg and John Shelby Spong are often named here; they would describe this as honest faith, not unbelief.

The key question that separates them is: what is the final measure? For progressive revelation, it is God’s self-disclosure in Jesus Christ, attested by the apostles. For many progressive Christians, it is the community’s developing conscience, which may read Jesus too as one stage on the road. In real life, views sit on a spectrum (see the visual), and people argue about where particular teachers belong. A fair reader names the measure each one actually uses, rather than labelling them.
49515:
The learner holds a strong Christ-centred view: Jesus is the full and final revelation of God, so the whole Bible must be read through him (“Jesus is perfect theology”). On this view, the Old Testament is a true, inspired and honest record of God working with people whose perception of him was still partial — “seeing through a glass, darkly”. Jesus is the moment God shows who he has been all along.

Defenders of this view (for example Greg Boyd, Brad Jersak and Brian Zahnd) insist that it is a form of progressive revelation, not progressive Christianity: the measure is not modern taste but the crucified and risen Christ. They also note that John 16 promises the Spirit will lead into “all truth” by taking what belongs to Jesus — not by moving beyond him.

Critics answer that, in practice, deciding what is “Christlike” can quietly import modern values, and that the line between the two can blur. Those debates come in lessons 17–19. For now, the point to hold is that the question “Is it Christlike?” and the question “Is it modern?” are different questions.

49517: How do later stages relate to earlier ones, and what is the final measure? Positions are rough; many people mix them.

49522: God reveals himself in stages; later stages complete earlier ones but never correct them. Every Old Testament statement about God is true for its stage, and Christ is the goal toward which it all moves.

49528: The Old Testament makes its full sense only when read backwards from the cross and resurrection. Christ is the goal (Greek *telos*) of the story, and the story keeps its own integrity as Israel’s story.

49539: Marcus Borg, John Shelby Spong (in different ways)
49540: Scripture is a human response to the sacred. Moral understanding grows through history, experience and science; many biblical teachings, and some traditional doctrines about Jesus, can be revised.

49608: Jon Levenson, Amy-Jill Levine, Marc Zvi Brettler

49612: “The Old Testament God and the New Testament God”
49613: The Old Testament shows an angry God of law and the New Testament shows a loving God of grace.
49614: Both Testaments speak of the same God who is “merciful and gracious, slow to anger” (Exod 34:6). Grace runs through the Old Testament (the exodus comes before the law), and judgement appears in the New. The real question is not two Gods but how God’s one character is revealed in stages and finally in Jesus. Jesus-lens writers such as Jersak and Boyd reject the “two Gods” idea just as firmly as traditional scholars do.
49615: Traditional scholars (e.g. Christopher J. H. Wright, Paul Copan) stress that the Old Testament is full of mercy and that the New Testament still speaks of wrath (John 3:36; Rom 1:18). They warn that the popular contrast repeats Marcion’s error.
49616: If we picture two Gods, we will either ignore half the Bible or fear the Father while loving the Son. Both Testaments ask us to know one God.
49617: “Progressive revelation means the Bible is out of date”
49618: If revelation is progressive, then later understanding (including ours) can correct the Bible.
49619: In Hebrews, the progression ends in the Son: God has spoken “in these last days” by him. The movement is toward Christ, not beyond him. Progressive revelation is a classic, conservative idea found in the church fathers and in Reformed theology.
49620: Many evangelical scholars add that later stages never contradict earlier ones; they complete them. Jesus-lens writers would agree that Christ is the end point, but they allow that people’s perception of God in some earlier texts was partial.
49621: Confusing the two words leads some to reject a healthy Christ-centred reading as “liberal”, and leads others to treat their own culture as the final word.

49630: Reading the Bible well (hermeneutics topic study)
49634: How Jesus and Paul Read the Scriptures
49635: How did Jesus and Paul bring clarity to the Old Testament Scriptures — and what does their way of reading teach us about how to read?
49636: Jesus did not read the Scriptures as a flat rule book. He read them as a story about himself, put mercy at the centre, named concessions as concessions, and sometimes said “but I say to you”. Paul, after meeting the risen Christ, said the same Scriptures stay veiled until we turn to the Lord.
49637: Jesus read the Scriptures as being about him
49638:
After the resurrection, Jesus walked with two discouraged disciples to Emmaus. “Beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself.” Later that evening he told the gathered disciples that everything written “in the law of Moses, and in the prophets, and in the psalms” about him had to be fulfilled — the three parts of the Hebrew Bible.

To religious leaders who knew the Scriptures well, he said: “Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me. And ye will not come to me, that ye might have life.” The problem was not too much Bible study. It was Bible study that never arrived at the person the Bible points to.

This is the starting point for everything else in this lesson: for Jesus, the Scriptures are a witness, and he is the one they witness to.
49639: “You have heard that it was said… but I say to you”
49640:
In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus says six times, “Ye have heard that it was said… but I say unto you.” Some of what “was said” is a direct quotation of the law (“thou shalt not kill”; “an eye for an eye”); some is a popular addition (“hate thine enemy” is not in the law). In each case Jesus goes deeper than the letter: from murder to anger, from adultery to lust, from limited revenge to no revenge, from loving neighbours to loving enemies.

Scholars read this in two main ways. Many evangelical and Jewish scholars say Jesus is not overturning Moses but recovering the law’s true intent against narrow interpretations — after all, he has just said he came “not to destroy, but to fulfil” and that not one stroke of the law will pass away. Others (including Jesus-lens writers) point out that in at least one case — “an eye for an eye” was God’s own legal command, not a misreading — Jesus moves beyond what the text required, speaking with an authority that belongs to God alone. The crowds noticed: he taught “as one having authority, and not as the scribes.”

Both readings agree on the heart of it: Jesus himself is the authoritative interpreter of the law, and the direction he takes it is toward the Father’s mercy — “that ye may be the children of your Father which is in heaven: for he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good.”
49641: Mercy as the key: Nazareth, Samaria and the dinner table
49642:
In the synagogue at Nazareth, Jesus read from Isaiah 61. He stopped in the middle of a sentence: after “to preach the acceptable year of the Lord”, he closed the scroll before the next words, “and the day of vengeance of our God”. Then he said, “This day is this scripture fulfilled in your ears.” Readers have long asked why he stopped there (see the lenses visual).

When a Samaritan village refused to welcome him, James and John asked whether they should call down fire from heaven — as Elijah had done to soldiers sent by King Ahaziah. Jesus “turned, and rebuked them.” Some later manuscripts add, “Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of”; the earliest manuscripts do not have these words, so most modern translations put them in a footnote. Either way, Jesus refused a method that one Old Testament story had used.

When he was criticised for eating with tax collectors and sinners, he quoted Hosea: “Go ye and learn what that meaneth, I will have mercy, and not sacrifice.” He quoted the same verse again when his disciples were accused of breaking the sabbath. “Go and learn” was a phrase teachers used for sending students back to a text; Jesus was telling experts in the Scriptures that they had missed the point of them.
49643: Concessions, foods and the sabbath: what the law was for
49644:
When asked about divorce, Jesus answered that “Moses because of the hardness of your hearts suffered you to put away your wives: but from the beginning it was not so.” Here Jesus himself says that a provision in the law of Moses was a concession to human hardness, not a picture of God’s ideal. He then reads Genesis 1–2 as the deeper word.

In Mark 7, Jesus teaches that what goes into a person does not make them unclean, but what comes out of the heart. Mark adds a comment: “Thus he declared all foods clean” (the wording of most modern translations; the KJV reads “purging all meats”). Acts shows the church taking time to grasp this. Jesus also said, “The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath” — the law serves human life, not the other way round.

Taken together, these show a pattern: Jesus asks what a command was for, and what it reveals about the Father’s heart. He keeps the law’s purpose and sets aside readings that work against it.
49645: Irony and sharp words against religious readings
49646:
The learner’s notes observe that Jesus used sarcasm and contradicted religious views. The Gospels show this clearly, though “irony” is often the more accurate word. “Full well ye reject the commandment of God, that ye may keep your own tradition” (Mark 7:9) is biting irony. “Ye blind guides, which strain at a gnat, and swallow a camel” is a comic picture of careful rule-keeping that misses “judgment, mercy, and faith”. “It cannot be that a prophet perish out of Jerusalem” is sharp irony about a city that kills its prophets.

Two cautions keep this fair. First, these were arguments inside Judaism, between Jews, in the style of the prophets — not attacks on Jewish people or on the Torah. Many Pharisees shared Jesus’ concern for mercy, and some later followed him. Second, Jesus’ target is a way of reading that uses Scripture to protect status and exclude others. Christians are just as capable of that today.
